title: Astroturfing
description: A campaign that makes coordinated promotion look like spontaneous support from ordinary people. Check who is behind a message and whether its sources are independent.

title: Bare assertion
description: A claim presented without evidence or reasoning to support it. Use the Claim Spotter to find checkable statements that may need sourcing.

title: Cherry-picking
description: Selecting only the evidence that supports a preferred conclusion while leaving out relevant contrary evidence. Compare the full set of data and sources, not just the examples shown.

title: Fabricated attribution
description: A statement is falsely assigned to a person or organization, or a source is invented. Verify quotations against the original publication or recording.

title: False dilemma
description: Presenting two choices as the only possibilities when other options or combinations exist. Ask what alternatives have been left out.

title: False balance
description: Giving two positions equal weight even when the amount or quality of evidence for them is very different. Look at the evidence and expert consensus, not just the number of voices.

title: Gish gallop
description: Overwhelming a discussion with many claims in quick succession, making each difficult to check. Break the argument into individual claims and assess them one at a time.

title: Motivated reasoning
description: The tendency to evaluate evidence in ways that favor a conclusion we already want to believe. Try stating what evidence would change your mind before reviewing the sources.

title: Survivorship bias
description: Drawing conclusions from the people or cases that remain visible while overlooking those that failed, disappeared or were never counted. Ask what is missing from the sample.

title: Clickbait
description: A headline designed to provoke curiosity or emotion, often by exaggerating or withholding key context. Compare the headline with what the article actually establishes.

title: Hedging
description: Language that qualifies how certain a statement is, such as “may” or “appears to.” It can accurately signal uncertainty, but vague hedges can also make a claim hard to assess.

title: Misleading statistics
description: Numbers presented without important context such as a baseline, sample size, time period or denominator. The Numbers-in-News Checker can flag some numerical patterns to examine.

title: Weasel words
description: Vague terms such as “experts say” or “many believe” that imply support without identifying who or how many. Ask for a named source and specific evidence.

title: Fact Check: Humans only use 10% of their brains.
description: Brain-damage, imaging and metabolic evidence reviewed in BMJ contradict the literal 10% claim; this does not mean every brain region is equally active at every moment.
keywords: do we only use 10 percent of our brain

title: Fact Check: The Great Wall of China is visible from space with the naked eye.
description: NASA says the Wall is not visible from the Moon and is difficult or impossible to see from Earth orbit without the high-powered lenses used for its photograph. The broad naked-eye claim needs this distance and viewing-condition qualification.
keywords: is the great wall of china visible from space

title: Fact Check: Earth's seasons are caused by its distance from the Sun.
description: NASA explains that seasonal weather patterns are mainly caused by Earth’s 23.5-degree axial tilt, not the elliptical orbit. Earth is near the Sun in January while the Northern Hemisphere is in winter.

title: Fact Check: The Moon has a permanently dark side.
description: NASA StarChild explains that the far side receives as much sunlight as the near side. A hemisphere hidden from Earth is not permanently unlit.

title: Fact Check: The flu shot can give you the flu.
description: CDC states that flu vaccines cannot cause flu illness: injected vaccines use inactivated viruses or a single viral protein. Side effects and infections acquired around vaccination are different from vaccine-caused flu.
keywords: can the flu shot give you the flu
